content:
CNN reports that Congressman Jamie Raskin sent a letter to Apple this week, challenging the company's explanation for removing ICEBlock from the App Store last year. Details below.

The ICEBlock removal incident is once again drawing attention

According to CNN, Apple sent a letter to Congressman Jamie Raskin last July explaining its decision to remove ICEBlock and similar apps from the App Store, and Raskin has now raised new questions about the company's rationale.

As background, ICEBlock is one of the most well-known apps that allows users to report and track ICE activity in their area. The app went viral during the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, with its user base surging from around 20,000 to roughly one million within a matter of weeks.

As its popularity soared, ICEBlock became a target of the US government, with then-Attorney General Pam Bondi publicly demanding that Apple remove the app and warning that its developer could face prosecution.

Following pressure from the Department of Justice, Apple removed the app and several similar apps from the App Store, citing concerns about the safety of federal law enforcement officers. The move came shortly before a gunman opened fire at a Dallas ICE facility, an incident that ultimately left two detainees dead and was classified by federal authorities as a deliberate act of violence targeting ICE.

This prompted Raskin to investigate whether the Trump administration had pressured Apple and Google to remove ICE-tracking apps, and what impact such removals might have on constitutionally protected free speech.

As part of the investigation, CNN reports that Apple sent a letter to Raskin last July explaining the reasons for removing ICEBlock and similar apps.

CNN reports:

Apple said its decision last year to remove ICEBlock and similar platforms from the App Store was driven by growing concerns about the safety of law enforcement officers following a deadly shooting at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement office in Dallas that left two detainees dead — concerns raised by the Trump administration were among them. Apple's explanation was contained in a July letter to Congressman Jamie Raskin. Raskin, a Maryland Democrat, currently serves as the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee. Raskin earlier this year launched an investigation into the Justice Department's role in the removal of such apps from Apple's and Google's app stores, as well as the implications for constitutionally protected free speech. The letter had not previously been reported.

CNN said the letter from Apple to Raskin also noted that the company had approved ICEBlock in April 2025, after its developer Joshua Aaron addressed what Apple described as "certain user privacy concerns."

Apple was also reported to have said that it continued to monitor news reports and criticism of the app in the following months, ultimately determining that ICEBlock and similar apps violated its App Store guidelines because they provided "precise location information about ICE personnel" that could potentially be used to carry out targeted attacks, and decided to remove them.

Apple also cited concerns raised by Bondi following the Dallas shooting, as well as remarks by FBI Director Kash Patel — who stated that the gunman had searched for an app capable of tracking ICE agents' locations.

According to Apple, these concerns, combined with what it described as an overall increase in activity targeting ICE and threats against law enforcement officers, prompted the company to launch a fresh review of ICEBlock.

Raskin pushes back

According to CNN, Raskin sent a letter to Apple this week further questioning the company's rationale for removing ICEBlock and similar apps.

Doug's top comment

Sounds like it's just for show. Apple found out the app was being used to target ICE, leading to some very serious confrontations and terrible consequences, so they chose to take it down. It's somewhat akin to how Facebook, Twitter and other platforms banned Trump's account after the January 6 incident. Not ideal, but they have the right to do it.

Nothing to see here……please move along……

CNN reports:

CNN also noted that Raskin pushed back against Apple's invocation of the Dallas shooting, arguing that the gunman did not need to use an ICE-tracking app to find a fixed government facility, and reportedly located the address through "an app preloaded on an Apple device."

He also pointed out that other navigation apps, while providing real-time information about law enforcement locations, remained available on the App Store, and demanded that Apple conduct a new independent review of its removal actions, as well as provide a complete list of all apps removed due to concerns raised by the Justice Department.
